introduction-it-doesnt-matter-if-the-ser.core: Users experience the whole chain: DNS, TLS, server response, then downloading, parsing and executing JavaScript, rendering, layout shifts and responsiveness to clicks on their own device and network. A 50 ms backend can still deliver a 6-second page on a mid-range phone over 3G. Frontend SRE extends SLOs and observability to the browser, where most of the user's wait often happens.

first_principles.problem: Backend p99 is 80 ms, yet users complain the app feels slow and conversion is falling.
truths: Most load time is often client-side.

analogy.title: A fast kitchen with a slow waiter
analogy.story: The food is cooked in two minutes, but diners wait 20 because of slow service between kitchen and table.
analogy.breaks: Waiters are one person; browsers are millions of different devices.

example.title: Where time goes
flow: JS bundle 1.8 MB download on 4G: 1.5 s

check.q: Why can a fast backend still produce a slow user experience?
check.a: Most time may be spent downloading, parsing and executing frontend code and rendering on slow devices and networks.

two-ways-to-measure-rum-vs-synthetics.core: Real User Monitoring (RUM) collects metrics from actual browsers via JavaScript (web-vitals, PerformanceObserver), capturing the true variety of devices, networks and behaviour, but it's noisy, needs traffic, and is limited by privacy. Synthetics run scripted browsers (Lighthouse, Playwright, WebPageTest) from controlled locations, which is consistent, good for baselines, pre-release testing and catching outages with no traffic, but not representative of real users. Use both.

first_principles.problem: Lighthouse scores are 95, but real users on Android in India see 6-second load times.
truths: Real data is noisy but true.
derivation: Run **synthetics in CI** to catch regressions.

analogy.title: Crash-test dummies vs real accident data
analogy.story: Lab tests are consistent; real-world data shows what actually happens to people.
analogy.breaks: Crash tests are expensive and rare; synthetics run every few minutes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Real field data segmented by page and network.

check.q: Why is p75 commonly used for Core Web Vitals field data?
check.a: It represents the experience of most users while being less noisy than higher percentiles; Google uses it for assessments.

core-web-vitals-the-google-standard.core: Core Web Vitals are Google's user-centric metrics. LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures loading, good at 2.5 s or less. INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures responsiveness, good at 200 ms or less. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures visual stability, good at 0.1 or less. They're assessed at the 75th percentile of real users and affect search ranking, giving a shared standard for frontend SLOs.

first_principles.problem: Product and engineering argue about 'fast' without an agreed definition.

analogy.title: A restaurant scored on wait, service and table wobble
analogy.story: How long until food arrives, how quickly staff respond, and whether the table keeps shifting.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants are judged by critics; CWV by real-user percentiles.

example.title: Frontend SLO
flow: SLI: share of page views with LCP ≤ 2.5 s

check.q: Which Core Web Vital replaced FID in 2024?
check.a: INP (Interaction to Next Paint), measuring overall responsiveness to interactions.

lcp-largest-contentful-paint.core: LCP marks when the largest visible element (hero image, heading, video poster) finishes rendering, a proxy for 'the main content has loaded'. It breaks down into TTFB, resource load delay (how late the browser discovers the image), resource load time, and render delay (blocked by CSS or JS). Fixes target each part: a fast server and CDN, preloading or fetchpriority for the hero, optimised images, and less render-blocking work.

first_principles.problem: The hero image loads late because it's injected by JavaScript after the bundle runs.
truths: Discovery delay is often the biggest part.

analogy.title: A theatre's main actor entering
analogy.story: The audience feels the show started when the lead appears; delays come from late arrival at the theatre, slow costume changes or the curtain being stuck.
analogy.breaks: Shows have one lead; LCP element varies by viewport and page.

check.q: Why should you never lazy-load the LCP image?
check.a: Lazy loading delays its fetch until layout, directly increasing LCP.

inp-interaction-to-next-paint.core: INP measures how quickly the page visually responds to clicks, taps and key presses: the latency from input to the next frame painted, reported near the worst interaction of a visit. Long tasks on the main thread (heavy JS, large re-renders, third-party scripts) delay processing. Fixes include breaking up long tasks (yielding with scheduler.yield or setTimeout), deferring non-urgent work, reducing JS, and virtualising large DOM updates.

first_principles.problem: Clicking 'Add to cart' freezes the page for 600 ms while analytics and re-render code run.

analogy.title: A receptionist who must finish filing before answering
analogy.story: Visitors wait at the desk until the current filing task is done.
analogy.breaks: Receptionists can pause; JS tasks don't yield unless coded to.

check.q: What's the main cause of poor INP?
check.a: Long tasks on the main thread that delay processing user input and painting the next frame.

cls-cumulative-layout-shift.core: CLS sums unexpected layout shifts, elements moving after they appeared, weighted by how much of the viewport moved and how far, with shifts grouped in session windows. Causes include images without dimensions, ads and embeds injected without reserved space, late-loading web fonts, and content inserted above existing content. Fixes: set width and height or aspect-ratio, reserve slots, use font-display with fallback metrics, and only shift in response to user input.

first_principles.problem: Users tap 'Buy' but an ad loads above it and they tap a different product instead.
derivation: Insert content **below** viewport or on interaction.

analogy.title: A bus that lurches as you reach for a handle
analogy.story: You aim for something and it moves at the last second.
analogy.breaks: Bus lurches are physical; CLS is a cumulative score.

check.q: Why don't layout shifts right after a user click count toward CLS?
check.a: Shifts within 500 ms of user input are expected responses, so they're excluded from the score.

containing-the-blast-error-boundaries.core: One JavaScript exception in a component can blank an entire single-page app. Error boundaries (React componentDidCatch or getDerivedStateFromError, and equivalents in other frameworks) catch render errors in a subtree and show a fallback, so a broken recommendations widget doesn't take down checkout. Combine them with global handlers (window.onerror, unhandledrejection) that report errors with context to tracking tools.

first_principles.problem: A null value in the reviews widget crashes the whole product page to a white screen.
truths: Uncaught render errors unmount the tree.
Non-critical features shouldn't break critical ones.
derivation: **Report** errors with route, release, user context.

analogy.title: Fire doors in a building
analogy.story: A fire in one room is contained so the rest of the building stays usable.
analogy.breaks: Fire doors stop all fires; boundaries don't catch event-handler or async errors.

check.q: What kinds of errors do React error boundaries not catch?
check.a: Errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (promises, timers), and server-side rendering.

the-debugging-gap-source-maps.core: Production JavaScript is minified and bundled, so stack traces look like 'a.js:1:48213 in t'. Source maps map minified positions back to original files, lines and names. Generate them in builds, upload them privately to the error-tracking tool tagged with the release version (rather than serving them publicly), and make sure the reported release matches, so errors show readable stacks.

first_principles.problem: Error reports show 'TypeError at main.8f3a.js:1:48213' and nobody can find the bug.
truths: Mappings can be generated at build time.

analogy.title: A key for a coded map
analogy.story: Without the key, symbols are meaningless; with it, you know exactly where everything is.
analogy.breaks: Map keys are universal; source maps must match the exact build.

code.text:
npm run build    # vite build --sourcemap hidden
npx @sentry/cli releases new "$GIT_SHA"
npx @sentry/cli sourcemaps upload --release "$GIT_SHA" ./dist/assets
npx @sentry/cli releases finalize "$GIT_SHA"
rm dist/assets/*.map    # don't deploy maps publicly

check.q: Why upload source maps privately instead of serving them with the site?
check.a: Public source maps expose original source code; private upload gives readable errors without revealing code.

the-frontend-observability-stack.core: A complete frontend stack has RUM (web vitals, navigation and resource timing, segmented by page, device, network and release), error tracking with source maps and breadcrumbs, synthetic checks for key journeys and CI performance budgets, session replay (privacy-masked) for hard bugs, and distributed tracing from browser to backend by propagating traceparent on fetch. Then frontend SLOs and alerts sit on top.

first_principles.problem: Frontend issues are discovered through customer support tickets days later.
truths: Browser signals are distinct from backend.

analogy.title: Flight data recorders for every passenger's journey
analogy.story: Each journey records timing, errors and the path through the airport, linked to the airline's back-office logs.
analogy.breaks: Flight recorders are mandatory; RUM must respect consent and privacy.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Click → fetch → backend spans in one trace.

check.q: What must be configured for browser fetch calls to join backend traces across origins?
check.a: Trace header propagation for those URLs, and CORS allowing the traceparent header on the API.
